questions.question: Which opening best reflects person-centered reproductive-life-planning care?
choices: Ask every patient whether they intend to become a parent before discussing any other concern
Ask privately what matters to the patient about pregnancy, pregnancy prevention, or parenting now or in the future, and whether they want to discuss it today
Recommend the most effective method before asking about the patient’s preferences
Avoid the topic unless the patient specifically asks for contraception
questions.explanation: A neutral, private, opt-in question respects reproductive autonomy and avoids assumptions about pregnancy desire, anatomy, identity, relationships, or parenting goals.

questions.question: A patient has a blood pressure of 162/104 and requests a combined estrogen-progestin pill. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Start the combined pill because the patient is younger than 35
Ignore the reading if the patient has no symptoms
Do not initiate combined hormonal contraception; assess the hypertension and discuss U.S. MEC-guided non-estrogen options
Give a three-month refill and recheck blood pressure only if symptoms occur
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable risk. The FNP should address the blood-pressure finding and preserve reproductive choice by discussing safer alternatives.

questions.question: Why does a history of migraine with aura require special caution before prescribing estrogen-containing contraception?
choices: Combined hormonal contraception is an unacceptable-risk option in migraine with aura, so non-estrogen alternatives should be considered using current guidance
Migraine with aura proves that no contraceptive method can be used
Aura changes only menstrual bleeding and has no vascular implication
A patient may use estrogen without assessment if headaches are infrequent
questions.explanation: Migraine with aura is a high-yield safety condition for combined hormonal contraception. Clarify the neurologic history and use current U.S. MEC guidance rather than treating all headaches as equivalent.

questions.question: A patient requests an IUD, but recent unprotected intercourse means the clinician cannot be reasonably certain the patient is not pregnant. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: A negative urine test today always excludes pregnancy after recent intercourse
IUD placement is appropriate as long as the patient has no symptoms
No contraceptive method can be discussed until the next menstrual period
Defer IUD placement until pregnancy can be reasonably excluded; some non-IUD methods may be quick-started with planned follow-up testing when clinically appropriate
questions.explanation: A urine pregnancy test has timing limitations. Current CDC guidance distinguishes IUD placement from several non-IUD methods when pregnancy cannot yet be reasonably excluded.

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient at risk for chlamydia and gonorrhea requests an IUD and is due for screening. What is the best general approach?
choices: Delay IUD placement until all screening results return, even if there are no symptoms
Obtain indicated screening the same day without automatically delaying placement, unless current purulent cervicitis or known active gonorrhea or chlamydia is present
Avoid all STI screening after IUD placement
Place the IUD only after giving empiric antibiotics to every patient
questions.explanation: Same-day screening can often occur without delaying IUD care in an asymptomatic patient. Current purulent cervicitis or known active gonorrhea or chlamydia changes the plan and requires treatment and follow-up.

questions.question: A patient presents three days after condom failure and does not want pregnancy. What is the priority?
choices: Offer time-sensitive emergency-contraception options promptly, assess safety and coercion privately, and create a follow-up and ongoing-contraception plan if desired
Wait until the next menstrual period before discussing options
Assume emergency contraception is not useful because a pregnancy test today is negative
Tell the patient emergency contraception terminates an established pregnancy
questions.explanation: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive. A pregnancy test today cannot erase the need to respond to recent exposure, and emergency contraception does not terminate an established pregnancy.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes, hypertension, and depression plans pregnancy and asks whether to stop all medications today. What is the safest response?
choices: Stop all medicines immediately because any medication is unsafe in pregnancy
Continue every medicine unchanged because preconception medication review is unnecessary
Delay any discussion until a pregnancy test becomes positive
Reconcile medications, assess disease control and pregnancy potential, then coordinate individualized changes with the relevant prescribers and obstetric specialists when indicated
questions.explanation: Some medicines need a planned transition, but abrupt discontinuation can cause serious maternal disease destabilization. Preconception care integrates medication safety with chronic-disease control and coordinated follow-up.

questions.question: What folic-acid counseling is appropriate for an average-risk person planning or capable of pregnancy?
choices: Take folic acid only after pregnancy is confirmed
Avoid folic acid unless there is a family history of neural-tube defects
Use daily folic acid 0.4 to 0.8 mg, or 400 to 800 micrograms, before conception and during early pregnancy; individualize higher-risk plans
Use the same high-dose plan for every patient without reviewing risk
questions.explanation: Current U.S. preventive guidance recommends 400 to 800 micrograms of folic acid daily for average-risk persons planning or capable of pregnancy. Higher-risk dosing requires individualized assessment.

questions.question: Which presentation requires emergency evaluation rather than a routine outpatient contraception follow-up?
choices: Possible pregnancy with severe unilateral pelvic pain, shoulder pain, presyncope, and heavy bleeding
A patient who wants to compare barrier and hormonal methods
Mild expected spotting after a recently started method without other symptoms
A patient asking whether a method can be discontinued
questions.explanation: Possible or confirmed pregnancy with severe pain, shoulder pain, syncope or presyncope, hypotension, or heavy bleeding raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or another emergency.

questions.question: A patient taking testosterone has pregnancy potential and does not want pregnancy. Which statement is correct?
choices: Testosterone is reliable contraception in all patients
Testosterone should not be treated as reliable contraception; provide nonjudgmental counseling based on pregnancy potential, goals, anatomy, and preferences
The topic should not be discussed unless the patient volunteers a gender identity label
Pregnancy potential can be inferred from appearance and relationship status
questions.explanation: Testosterone is not reliable contraception. Inclusive reproductive care uses clinically relevant, respectful questions rather than assumptions about identity, anatomy, or sexual practices.
